ULTRASOUND__Abdomen:
General abdominal ultrasound (US) is the first-line cross-sectional test for a huge range of abdominal problems — right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, jaundice, deranged LFTs, a palpable mass, and renal impairment. It is safe, cheap, portable and dynamic, but it is highly operator-dependent and easily defeated by bowel gas and body habitus. Learn the vocabulary of echoes and what a standard scan does — and does not — reliably show.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
1The physical principle
A transducer emits high-frequency sound waves (well above audible range) into the body. At each tissue interface, some of the wave is reflected back as an echo; the machine times these echoes and converts their strength and depth into a real-time, cross-sectional greyscale image. Because it is live, US shows movement (peristalsis, blood flow with Doppler, a sliding lung) and can guide needles during procedures. No ionising radiation is involved.
2Echogenicity — reading the greyscale
Structures are described by how brightly they reflect sound: hyperechoic (bright — fat, gallstones, calcification, fibrosis), hypoechoic (darker than surrounding tissue), and anechoic (completely black — simple fluid such as a cyst, the full bladder, or ascites). Two classic artefacts help you interpret: acoustic shadowing — a dark band behind a strongly reflective/absorbing structure (stone, calcification, gas); and posterior acoustic enhancement — a bright band behind a fluid-filled structure because sound passes through fluid with little attenuation.
Bright focus + shadow behind it in the gallbladder→Gallstone
Anechoic + posterior enhancement — simple cyst or fluid
Hyperechoic + acoustic shadow — stone, calcification or gas
Bright, enlarged liver, poor deep detail — fatty infiltration (steatosis)
3What a standard abdominal scan covers
A general abdominal US surveys the liver (size, texture, focal lesions), gallbladder and biliary tree (stones, wall thickening, duct dilatation), pancreas (frequently obscured by overlying bowel gas), spleen (size), kidneys (size, cortical thickness, hydronephrosis, stones), aorta (calibre — screening for aneurysm), and any free fluid. Patients are usually fasted, which lets the gallbladder distend and makes stones and wall pathology far easier to see.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
4Strengths and limitations
The advantages are why US is first-line: no ionising radiation (safe, repeatable, ideal in pregnancy and children), cheap, portable/bedside, real-time and dynamic, and it enables image-guided procedures (drains, biopsies). The limitations are equally important to quote: it is operator-dependent, degraded by bowel gas and obesity (body habitus), poor for the retroperitoneum and pancreas (CT is superior), and offers only a small field of view.
🔊Anechoic
Black on screen — simple fluid: cyst, full bladder, ascites.
⬛Shadowing
Dark band behind stone, calcification or gas.
💡Enhancement
Bright band behind a fluid-filled structure (cyst).
💨Gas defeats US
Bowel gas blocks sound — pancreas often unseen.
🚩
US is often the triage test. A positive finding — dilated ducts, a mass, or free fluid — directs onward CT/MRI or urgent referral. Do not rely on a "normal" US to exclude serious pathology when clinical suspicion is high; a gas-obscured pancreas or a lesion outside the field of view can be missed.
🎓 Exam pearl. "Bright with a shadow behind it" = stone/calcification; "black with brightening behind it" = simple fluid/cyst. And always pair US's strengths (no radiation, bedside, dynamic) with its Achilles heels (operator-dependent, bowel gas, obesity, poor pancreas) — examiners love the trade-off.

Ultrasound is the first-line imaging test for the liver: cheap, radiation-free, and quick. It is the go-to investigation for abnormal LFTs, hepatomegaly, RUQ pain, and 6-monthly HCC surveillance in cirrhosis. It excels at telling diffuse disease from focal disease and cystic from solid — but often cannot definitively characterise a solid lesion, so anything indeterminate or suspicious proceeds to contrast-enhanced CT or MRI.

1Diffuse disease — read the whole parenchyma

Compare the liver's brightness to the adjacent right kidney cortex. Normally they are similar; if the liver is brighter, suspect fat.

Bright/hyperechoic liver + posterior beam attenuation + blurred vessels & diaphragm→FATTY LIVER (steatosis / NAFLD) — the classic "bright liver"
Coarse echotexture + nodular surface + small shrunken liver (or enlarged caudate/left lobe)→CIRRHOSIS — look for portal hypertension

Signs of portal hypertension to actively hunt for:

Splenomegaly (spleen > 12 cm) — the most reproducible sign
Ascites — anechoic free fluid in Morison's pouch and pelvis
Dilated portal vein (> 13 mm) and a recanalised umbilical vein
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image showing a bright, hyperechoic "fatty liver" with posterior beam attenuation, the diaphragm poorly seen, next to the darker right kidney for comparison.
2Focal lesions — cystic vs solid

The first branch point for any focal lesion is whether it is cystic (fluid) or solid — this changes the differential and the next step entirely.

💧Simple cyst
Anechoic (black), thin imperceptible wall, posterior acoustic enhancement. Benign — no follow-up needed.
🔴Haemangioma
Well-defined, uniformly hyperechoic (bright). Commonest benign solid lesion — often an incidental finding.
🎯Metastases
Often multiple; classic "target"/bull's-eye lesion (hypoechoic rim). Commonest malignant liver lesion.
❓Indeterminate solid
Any solid lesion US cannot confidently label → characterise with contrast-enhanced CT or MRI.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image of a simple hepatic cyst: an anechoic round lesion with a thin wall and bright posterior acoustic enhancement behind it.
3Surveillance & Doppler

HCC surveillance: patients with cirrhosis get 6-monthly ultrasound (± serum AFP). A new solid nodule in a surveillance scan is a red flag and warrants further cross-sectional imaging.

New solid nodule in a cirrhotic liver→Assume possible HCC — multiphase CT/MRI

Doppler of the portal vein assesses flow direction (normal hepatopetal, towards the liver; reversed/hepatofugal flow indicates severe portal hypertension) and can detect portal vein thrombosis (echogenic material filling the lumen with absent flow).

🚩 A new focal solid lesion in a cirrhotic liver is HCC until proven otherwise — refer and arrange contrast CT/MRI. Also escalate any features of decompensated liver disease or portal hypertension (new ascites, reversed portal flow, portal vein thrombosis).
🎓 Ultrasound detects liver lesions brilliantly but frequently cannot characterise a solid one. Cystic + anechoic + posterior enhancement = reassure; solid + indeterminate = cross-sectional imaging. Never let a normal-looking bright liver distract you from the surface nodularity and splenomegaly that betray established cirrhosis.

Ultrasound is the gold-standard first-line investigation for suspected gallstones and gallbladder disease. It is cheap, radiation-free and highly sensitive for stones. Reach for it in the patient with right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, colicky post-prandial pain, or deranged liver function tests (LFTs), and use it to answer three questions: are there stones, is the gallbladder inflamed, and are the bile ducts obstructed?

1
Gallstones (cholelithiasis)

The classic triad on ultrasound: a mobile, hyperechoic (bright) focus within the gallbladder lumen that casts posterior acoustic shadowing and moves with gravity/position (rolls to the dependent part when the patient turns). The shadow occurs because the stone reflects and absorbs the sound beam, leaving a dark band behind it. Mobility distinguishes a stone from a fixed polyp; shadowing distinguishes it from sludge or a polyp.

Bright focus + posterior shadow + moves with position→Gallstone
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: a bright echogenic focus in the dependent gallbladder lumen with a clean dark posterior acoustic shadow extending beneath it.
2
Acute cholecystitis

Look for the inflammatory signs: gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder distension, and a stone impacted in the neck or cystic duct (the obstructing culprit). The bedside clincher is a positive sonographic Murphy's sign — maximal tenderness elicited as the probe is pressed directly over the gallbladder, more specific than the clinical Murphy's sign because the point of tenderness is localised under direct vision.

Wall >3 mm thick
Pericholecystic fluid
Distended gallbladder
Stone in neck/cystic duct
Positive sonographic Murphy's

Watch for complications: a striated/irregular or non-enhancing wall and intraluminal membranes suggest gangrenous cholecystitis; gas within the wall or lumen (bright foci with dirty shadowing) indicates emphysematous cholecystitis; a fluid-filled, pus-distended gallbladder is an empyema; and loss of wall continuity with adjacent collection signals perforation.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: a distended gallbladder with a thickened oedematous wall (>3 mm), a thin rim of pericholecystic fluid, and a stone lodged in the gallbladder neck.
3
Biliary obstruction & the CBD

When LFTs show an obstructive picture, measure the common bile duct (CBD). A dilated CBD (>6–7 mm, allowing roughly 1 mm per decade over 60, and wider post-cholecystectomy) suggests obstruction — a stone in the duct (choledocholithiasis), a stricture, or a tumour. Also look for intrahepatic duct dilatation (branching tubular structures paralleling portal veins, the "parallel channel" sign). Crucially, ultrasound is less sensitive for the CBD stones themselves (bowel gas obscures the distal duct), so if a duct stone is suspected proceed to MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).

Dilated CBD >6–7 mm + obstructive LFTs→Obstruction → MRCP/EUS

Mirizzi syndrome is extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by a stone impacted in the cystic duct/Hartmann's pouch, causing obstructive jaundice with a normal-calibre distal CBD.

4
Polyps, carcinoma & other findings

Gallbladder polyps are non-mobile, non-shadowing soft-tissue projections from the wall; most are benign, but size (>10 mm), rapid growth or associated gallstones raise concern. Gallbladder carcinoma (rare) shows focal/asymmetric wall thickening or a mass replacing the lumen. A porcelain gallbladder (calcified wall — a bright curvilinear rim with dense shadowing) carries a malignancy association and warrants surgical discussion.

💎
Gallstone
Mobile, shadowing, bright — moves with position.
🔺
Polyp
Fixed, non-shadowing wall projection — no movement.
🌫️
Sludge
Low-level mobile echoes, no shadow, layers dependently.
🏺
Porcelain GB
Calcified wall, bright rim, dense shadow — malignancy link.
🚩 Ascending cholangitis is an emergency. Charcot's triad — fever, RUQ pain and jaundice (with a dilated CBD on ultrasound) — signals infection of an obstructed biliary tree. It needs prompt IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP); deterioration to Reynolds' pentad (adding hypotension and confusion) marks septic shock. Distinguish from acute cholecystitis, which requires admission, antibiotics and (laparoscopic) cholecystectomy — cholecystitis inflames the gallbladder, cholangitis infects the ducts.
🎓 Pearl: Ultrasound is superb at showing stones in the gallbladder but poor at showing stones in the duct. So when the LFTs are obstructive and the CBD is dilated but you can't see the culprit stone, don't call it normal — the answer is MRCP or EUS, not repeat ultrasound.

The pancreas sits retroperitoneally and is frequently obscured by overlying bowel gas, so transabdominal ultrasound of the gland is limited. CT is the main cross-sectional test for pancreatic disease — remember US here mostly to hunt for a gallstone cause of pancreatitis, not to assess the gland itself.

1Why the pancreas is a hard US target

Deep and retroperitoneal, lying anterior to the aorta/IVC and behind the stomach and transverse colon. Gas in overlying bowel scatters the beam, so the body and especially the tail are often not seen. A fasted patient and the fluid-filled stomach as an acoustic window help, but coverage stays incomplete.

Gland poorly visualised / question of complications→CT is the cross-sectional test of choice
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
2Acute pancreatitis — US looks for the CAUSE

Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis is clinical + amylase/lipase, NOT imaging. The job of US is to find a treatable gallstone aetiology — the commonest cause alongside alcohol. Look in the gallbladder and CBD.

Gallstones in the gallbladder + a dilated CBD → gallstone pancreatitis.
Oedematous, enlarged, hypoechoic gland; peripancreatic free fluid.
CT (ideally at 48–72h) grades severity and detects necrosis and complications far better than US.
Gallstones + dilated CBD in acute pancreatitis→Gallstone pancreatitis — consider ERCP if obstructed
3Pattern recognition on US
💧Pseudocyst
Well-defined anechoic collection, usually >4 weeks after acute pancreatitis.
🪨Chronic pancreatitis
Atrophic gland, echogenic calcifications with shadowing, dilated pancreatic duct.
🎯Head mass
Hypoechoic mass in the head with double-duct sign (dilated CBD + pancreatic duct).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
4Suspected pancreatic cancer

A hypoechoic head mass causing biliary and pancreatic duct dilatation (double-duct sign) raises adenocarcinoma. US may be the first test that spots it, but endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) and CT are far superior for detection, staging and biopsy.

Painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss→Urgent CT / EUS referral for suspected pancreatic cancer
🚩 Severe / necrotising pancreatitis (organ failure, SIRS) is life-threatening — use CT for necrosis and complications, do not rely on US. Painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss is pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise.
🎓 On the wards, treat pancreatic US as a gallstone-hunting tool in acute pancreatitis, not a way to diagnose it or assess the gland. If you need to see the pancreas itself — severity, necrosis, a mass, staging — reach for CT (and EUS for tissue).

The spleen is a superficial left-upper-quadrant organ that ultrasound assesses well: is it enlarged, does it contain focal lesions, and — in trauma — is there free blood? US is the first-line, radiation-free bedside tool, but remember its two big limitations: it is operator-dependent, and in unstable trauma it never delays the trip to theatre.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image. Normal spleen: homogeneous, mildly hyperechoic to renal cortex, crescentic organ imaged in the left intercostal/coronal plane, with the diaphragm above and left kidney inferomedial; measure the longest bipolar length.
1Measure the length — is it splenomegaly?
Measure the maximum bipolar (cranio-caudal) length in the coronal plane through the hilum. Normal is <12–13 cm. Above this = splenomegaly. Also note the normal homogeneous echotexture (slightly more echogenic than adjacent renal cortex) and scan for focal lesions.
Spleen >13 cm, tip reaching below costal margin / crossing midline→splenomegaly — hunt for a cause and for focal deposits
2Work through the causes of splenomegaly
A structured list keeps you safe under questioning:
Portal hypertension — cirrhosis; look for coarse liver, ascites, recanalised umbilical vein and reversed portal flow on Doppler.
Haematological malignancy — lymphoma, chronic leukaemias (esp. CML) — often massive splenomegaly.
Infection — infectious mononucleosis (EBV), malaria, and other tropical/chronic infections.
Haemolytic anaemias — hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia, sickle cell (early; later autosplenectomy).
Infiltration — amyloid, sarcoid, storage disorders (e.g. Gaucher).
3Focal splenic lesions
Characterise any focal abnormality:
Cyst — anechoic, thin-walled, posterior acoustic enhancement.
Infarct — classically wedge-shaped, peripheral, hypoechoic, base to the capsule; think endocarditis (septic emboli) or sickle cell.
Abscess — complex hypoechoic collection ± gas/debris in a septic patient.
Lymphomatous deposits — hypoechoic nodules (rare but classic).
Accessory spleen (splenunculus) — small round nodule near the hilum with identical echotexture; a normal variant, do not mistake for a mass or lymph node.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image. FAST view of the left upper quadrant (splenorenal recess): anechoic (black) fluid tracking between spleen and left kidney and around the splenic tip indicating free intraperitoneal blood.
4The spleen in blunt abdominal trauma
The spleen is the commonest solid organ injured in blunt abdominal trauma. As part of the FAST scan, US looks for free intraperitoneal fluid (haemoperitoneum) in the splenorenal recess and pelvis, and may show a laceration or subcapsular haematoma. Crucially, US tells you whether there is free fluid, not the full injury grade.
Positive FAST + haemodynamically UNSTABLE→resuscitate and go straight to theatre — do NOT wait for CT
Haemodynamically STABLE trauma patient→CT is the definitive test to grade injury and plan conservative management
📏Splenomegaly
Length >12–13 cm; confirm and hunt for focal deposits and a cause.
🩸FAST / trauma
Detects free fluid; unstable → theatre, stable → CT to grade.
🔺Infarct
Wedge-shaped peripheral hypoechoic lesion; think emboli/sickle cell.
🚩 Splenic injury or rupture with haemodynamic instability is a surgical emergency. Resuscitate and transfer to theatre — do NOT delay for CT. Consider splenic rupture in any patient with recent trauma or infectious mononucleosis (EBV) who presents with left-upper-quadrant pain, left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign) and signs of shock.
🎓 In infectious mononucleosis the spleen is enlarged and fragile, so patients are advised to avoid contact sports (typically for ~3–4 weeks / until recovery) because of the risk of atraumatic or minor-trauma splenic rupture. A soft, homogeneously enlarged spleen with a viral illness in a young adult is EBV until proven otherwise.
ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta & Acute:
Renal ultrasound is the first-line imaging test for acute kidney injury (AKI), suspected obstruction, visible haematuria, renal masses and chronic kidney disease. It is quick, radiation-free and portable — but its single most important job in the acutely unwell patient is to answer one binary question: is the collecting system obstructed?

1Hydronephrosis — the obstruction question

Hydronephrosis is dilatation of the pelvicalyceal system, seen on US as anechoic (black) branching fluid filling and expanding the central renal sinus. In AKI the reflex question is "is there a post-renal cause?" — because obstruction is reversible if decompressed early.

Bilateral hydronephrosis (or unilateral in a single functioning kidney) + rising creatinine→obstructive (post-renal) AKI needing urgent decompression via nephrostomy or ureteric stent

Grade the dilatation (mild pelvic fullness through to gross ballooning with cortical thinning) and hunt for the level and cause: an obstructing stone, a pelvic/ureteric mass, or bladder outlet obstruction. Always image the bladder and prostate and measure a post-void residual — a chronically distended bladder with bilateral hydronephrosis points to outlet obstruction rather than a ureteric lesion.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
2Stones, cysts and cystic disease

A renal stone appears as a bright echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing. US reliably detects renal-pelvis stones and the hydronephrosis they cause, but CT KUB is more sensitive, especially for ureteric stones which US often misses.

Simple cyst (Bosniak I): anechoic, thin imperceptible wall, posterior acoustic enhancement — benign, no follow-up.
Complex cyst: septa, calcification, wall thickening or solid components — needs CT/MRI characterisation.
ADPKD: multiple bilateral cysts with enlarged kidneys and distorted architecture.

Posterior enhancement (increased through-transmission behind a cyst) confirms the lesion is fluid-filled; its presence helps distinguish a simple cyst from a solid mass.

3Renal masses and chronic change

Any solid renal mass on US is a possible renal cell carcinoma (RCC) until proven otherwise and mandates CT characterisation and staging plus urology referral. An angiomyolipoma is a benign fat-containing tumour that looks strikingly echogenic (bright) — but overlap with small RCCs means CT is still used to confirm macroscopic fat.

🔊CKD kidney
Small, echogenic (bright cortex), cortical thinning, loss of corticomedullary differentiation — bilateral small kidneys imply chronicity and irreversibility.
🩻Solid mass
Heterogeneous solid lesion — assume RCC; CT staging and urology referral.
🫘Transplant
Doppler assessment of arterial/venous flow and resistive index — screens for rejection, ATN and vascular complications.

In CKD the distinction matters: bilateral small echogenic kidneys signal established, irreversible disease and steer away from aggressive investigation, whereas normal-sized kidneys keep acute or potentially reversible causes on the table.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
🚩 An obstructed, infected kidney (pyonephrosis) — or bilateral obstruction with AKI — is a urological emergency: pus under pressure causes rapid sepsis and irreversible renal loss, and needs urgent decompression (nephrostomy/stent), not just antibiotics. Separately, any solid renal mass = possible RCC → CT plus urology referral.
🎓 In every AKI, the ultrasound exists to answer one question first — "is there hydronephrosis?" A normal, unobstructed system with normal-sized kidneys reassures you the cause is pre-renal or intrinsic; bilateral dilatation flips the patient into an obstructive pathway where a nephrostomy can rescue the kidneys within hours.

Ultrasound is the frontline test for detecting and monitoring the abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) — cheap, quick, radiation-free, and reliable at measuring the maximal aortic diameter. It underpins the NHS AAA Screening Programme and all subsequent surveillance.

1Define the AAA

An AAA is an aortic diameter ≥3 cm, measured outer-to-outer in the anteroposterior plane. Ultrasound measures this maximal diameter reliably at the bedside. Most AAAs are infrarenal and fusiform (symmetrical dilatation of the whole circumference).

AP diameter ≥3 cm outer-to-outer→aneurysm — enter surveillance
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
2Screen and survey

The NHS AAA Screening Programme offers a one-off abdominal ultrasound to men in the year they turn 65. Because US is cheap, fast and involves no radiation, it is ideal for both screening and repeated surveillance.

Small (3.0–4.4 cm): rescan yearly.
Medium (4.5–5.4 cm): rescan 3-monthly.
Look for mural thrombus lining the sac — common and does not protect against rupture.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
3When to refer

Refer to vascular surgery for consideration of elective repair when any of the following apply:

📏Diameter ≥5.5 cm
Rupture risk rises steeply above this threshold.
📈Rapid expansion
Growth >1 cm per year on surveillance.
⚠️Symptomatic
Any abdominal/back pain or tenderness attributable to the AAA.

Repair is either open surgical (graft) or endovascular (EVAR), with the choice guided by anatomy and fitness.

4US vs CT — pick the right test

Ultrasound is the screening and surveillance tool. CT angiography is used for pre-operative planning and to diagnose rupture in a stable patient — it maps the neck, iliac vessels and relation to renal arteries (key for EVAR sizing).

Stable patient, planning repair→CT angiography
🚩 Ruptured AAA — the classic triad is sudden severe abdominal/back pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass, and hypotension/collapse. A haemodynamically unstable patient with a known or suspected AAA goes straight to theatre — do NOT delay for CT. Bedside POCUS can confirm the aneurysm in seconds.
🎓 Remember the size ladder: 3.0–4.4 cm yearly, 4.5–5.4 cm 3-monthly, ≥5.5 cm refer. US finds and follows; CT plans and confirms rupture in the stable; the crashing patient bypasses imaging and goes to theatre.

Ultrasound is exquisitely sensitive for intraperitoneal free fluid — it detects even small volumes long before clinical shifting dullness appears. Fluid is anechoic (jet-black) and collects in the most dependent recesses, making US the first-line tool to confirm ascites, estimate its volume, characterise it, and safely guide a paracentesis needle.

1Recognise free fluid — anechoic, dependent, no wall
Free fluid is black (anechoic), has no capsule or wall of its own, and pools where gravity takes it. Scan the dependent spaces: Morison's pouch (hepatorenal recess, between liver and right kidney), the perisplenic space (splenorenal recess), around the liver edge, and the pelvis / pouch of Douglas. Fluid tracks around loops of bowel, which appear to float within it.
Anechoic stripe in Morison's pouch→free fluid — the earliest and most sensitive site in a supine patient
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: RUQ view showing an anechoic (black) triangular stripe of fluid in Morison's pouch, sitting in the hepatorenal recess between the liver and right kidney.
2Simple vs complex fluid — read the echoes
The character of the fluid narrows the cause. Simple / transudative ascites is uniformly anechoic. Complex fluid contains internal echoes, debris, septations or loculation, which suggests exudate, infection, haemorrhage or malignancy.
Uniformly anechoic, free-flowing → simple transudate (e.g. cirrhosis, heart failure)
Internal echoes / debris → haemoperitoneum, infected or malignant fluid
Septations / loculation → TB peritonitis, malignant deposits, chronic infection
3Frame the cause — transudate vs exudate by SAAG
Divide causes by the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) = serum albumin − ascitic albumin. A high gradient means portal hypertension is driving the fluid.
💧SAAG ≥11 g/L (transudate)
Portal hypertension: cirrhosis (commonest cause overall), heart failure, Budd-Chiari.
🧫SAAG <11 g/L (exudate)
Non-portal: malignancy / peritoneal deposits, infection / TB, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome.
4Guide the tap — safer than blind
US marks a safe pocket of fluid clear of bowel, bladder and vessels — bedside US-guided paracentesis is safer than a blind tap. The classic site is the left iliac fossa, but always avoid the inferior epigastric arteries (which run up the rectus sheath), any dilated superficial veins, and the distended bladder. A diagnostic ascitic tap samples fluid for cell count, albumin, protein, culture and cytology; therapeutic drainage relieves tense ascites.
Any new-onset ascites, or a cirrhotic who decompensates→diagnostic tap to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: a large anechoic pocket of ascites in the left iliac fossa with free-floating bowel loops, marked as a safe target for paracentesis away from bowel and vessels.
5Beyond ascites — trauma and haemoperitoneum
The same principle underlies the FAST scan (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma): free fluid in Morison's pouch, the splenorenal recess, the pelvis or around the heart in an injured patient represents haemoperitoneum until proven otherwise. In an unstable trauma patient, positive free fluid mandates urgent surgical review.
🚩 Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) — fever, abdominal pain or unexplained encephalopathy in a cirrhotic is a medical emergency. It is confirmed by ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm³ and needs a prompt diagnostic tap plus empirical antibiotics. Separately, free fluid in a trauma or haemodynamically unstable patient suggests haemoperitoneum requiring immediate resuscitation and surgical input.
🎓 The three questions US answers about free fluid: Is it there? (anechoic stripe in Morison's pouch — most sensitive), What is it? (simple vs complex echoes), and Can I safely tap it? (mark a pocket clear of bowel and the inferior epigastric arteries). Never send home a new ascites or a decompensating cirrhotic without a diagnostic tap — you are excluding SBP.

Appendicitis is a clinical diagnosis — RIF pain, migratory (central → right iliac fossa) pain, anorexia, low-grade fever and localised peritonism. Imaging earns its place only when the diagnosis is uncertain. Ultrasound with graded compression is the first-line scan whenever ionising radiation is best avoided: children, young women and pregnancy.

1When ultrasound is first-line
Reach for US before CT in three groups: children (radiation-sensitive), young women / women of childbearing age (also interrogates the ovaries and adnexa in one sitting) and pregnancy. Always send a pregnancy test in any woman of childbearing age with RIF pain to exclude ectopic before you image.
Young woman, RIF pain, diagnosis unclear→Graded-compression US first (bowel + gynae in one look)
2Positive US features of acute appendicitis
Track the tubular structure back to the caecal pole and confirm it is blind-ending. The diagnostic combination is a non-compressible, aperistaltic tube with a diameter >6 mm.
Cross-section shows a "target" sign — concentric gut-wall layers.
An appendicolith is echogenic with posterior acoustic shadowing.
Periappendiceal fluid and inflamed echogenic fat surround the appendix.
Hyperaemia of the wall on colour Doppler.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: longitudinal view of a blind-ending, non-compressible tubular structure arising from the caecal pole, diameter measured >6 mm.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: transverse "target" sign of the inflamed appendix with a shadowing appendicolith and surrounding echogenic inflamed fat.
3Complications to name on the scan
💥Perforation
Loss of wall integrity, free fluid, focal collection — a surgical emergency.
🧱Mass / phlegmon
Inflamed appendix walled off by omentum and adjacent bowel.
🩸Abscess
Organised, thick-walled fluid collection — may need drainage.
4The key limitation
US is operator-dependent and a non-visualised appendix does NOT exclude appendicitis — it can rule in, but it cannot rule out. If US is negative or equivocal yet clinical suspicion persists, escalate: CT in adults, MRI in pregnancy, or observation / diagnostic laparoscopy. Keep differentials in mind: mesenteric adenitis, ovarian pathology / torsion, ectopic pregnancy and Meckel's diverticulitis.
US shows no appendix but pain and signs persist→Do NOT discharge — CT (adult) / MRI (pregnant) / observe / laparoscopy
🚩 Perforated appendicitis with generalised peritonitis or sepsis is a surgical emergency: resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and proceed to appendicectomy. In any woman of childbearing age with RIF pain, a pregnancy test is mandatory to exclude ectopic before you commit to a diagnosis.
🎓 A positive scan confirms, but a normal scan never clears: the appendix is a small, mobile, gas-obscured structure, so a non-visualised appendix on US in a child, young woman or pregnant patient with a convincing story means you keep looking — not that you send them home.
ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gynae:
Transabdominal ultrasound (TAUS) is the first-line, non-invasive pelvic scan. A low-frequency curvilinear probe is placed suprapubically, and a full bladder is used as an acoustic window — the distended, fluid-filled bladder pushes gas-filled bowel out of the way and provides a clear interface through which the uterus, ovaries and adnexa can be seen.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: midline sagittal suprapubic view showing the anechoic (black) full bladder anteriorly, with the pear-shaped uterus lying behind it and the linear echogenic endometrial stripe visible centrally.
1Why the full bladder matters
The single most important preparation step. Bowel gas scatters ultrasound and hides the pelvic organs; a full bladder solves this in two ways.
Distended bladder→displaces gas-filled bowel loops out of the pelvis
Fluid-filled bladder→acts as an acoustic window, transmitting sound to deeper structures
Ask the patient to drink ~1 litre of water and hold urine before the scan.
An empty bladder gives a technically poor, often non-diagnostic study.
2What TAUS assesses
A panoramic sweep of the pelvis in sagittal and transverse planes.
🍐Uterus
Size, position (anteverted vs retroverted), fibroids, and endometrial thickness (assessed less reliably than on transvaginal).
🥚Ovaries & adnexa
Ovarian size, cysts and adnexal masses — better seen when large or extending out of the pelvis.
💧Pouch of Douglas
Free fluid in the rectouterine pouch — may reflect physiological fluid, blood or pus.
🫧Bladder
Wall, volume and post-void residual — the acoustic window is also the organ examined.
3Strengths vs limitations
TAUS trades resolution for reach and acceptability.
Advantages: non-invasive, gives a panoramic overview, ideal for large masses that extend beyond the pelvis, acceptable to all patients, and the first-line choice in children and virgins where transvaginal (TV) scanning is inappropriate.
Limitations: lower resolution than TV; images degraded by obesity and bowel gas; useless with an empty bladder; a retroverted uterus is difficult to visualise.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: transverse suprapubic view with the full bladder anteriorly and both ovaries visualised laterally, each containing several small anechoic follicles.
4Order of use — TAUS then TV
TAUS and transvaginal scanning are complementary, not competing. TAUS gives the wide overview; TV gives a high-resolution close-up because the probe sits right next to the organs.
Standard pelvic assessment→TAUS overview first, then TV for detailed resolution
🚩 In acute pelvic pain or suspected ectopic pregnancy, a technically limited or empty-bladder TAUS does not exclude pathology. A normal-looking transabdominal scan is falsely reassuring — proceed to transvaginal ultrasound before ruling out an ectopic or significant adnexal disease.
🎓 Remember the bladder does double duty on TAUS: it is both the acoustic window (full = good images) and one of the organs assessed. If the pictures are poor, the first question is always "is the bladder full enough?" — and if the answer stays no in an unwell patient, escalate to transvaginal rather than accepting a normal report.

Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) puts a high-frequency probe directly into the vagina, sitting millimetres from the pelvic organs. That proximity buys resolution: it is the gold-standard scan for endometrial thickness, small ovarian lesions, follicle tracking and — crucially — early and ectopic pregnancy. One counter-intuitive rule up front: unlike transabdominal scanning, TVUS needs an empty bladder.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: sagittal TVUS of a normal anteverted uterus with a thin bright endometrial stripe and posterior cervix, probe marker at the fundus.
1Why transvaginal beats transabdominal

A higher-frequency probe placed closer to the target trades penetration for detail. Transabdominal scanning (full bladder acting as an acoustic window) surveys the whole pelvis and large masses; TVUS gives the close-up. For endometrial measurement, tiny ovarian follicles, early gestational sacs and adnexal detail, TVUS wins.

Need fine detail of endometrium, ovaries or early pregnancy→transvaginal, empty bladder
Large mass, overview, or TVUS not tolerated/appropriate→transabdominal, full bladder
Empty bladder before the scan — a full bladder pushes the pelvic organs out of the probe's near field and degrades the image.
2Early pregnancy and the discriminatory zone

A gestational sac becomes visible on TVUS from roughly 5 weeks, correlating with a serum hCG above the discriminatory zone (~1500 IU/L). Seeing an intrauterine gestational sac (ideally with yolk sac) confirms an intrauterine pregnancy and makes ectopic very unlikely.

hCG > ~1500 IU/L but no intrauterine sac seen→worry about ectopic / PUL
Confirmed intrauterine pregnancy → ectopic essentially excluded (heterotopic rare, higher risk with IVF).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: TVUS of an early intrauterine pregnancy showing a round anechoic gestational sac eccentrically placed within the endometrium with a bright yolk sac ring.
3Endometrium in postmenopausal bleeding

Any postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise, and TVUS endometrial thickness is the first-line triage. A stripe <4–5 mm is reassuring; a thickened endometrium mandates hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy.

Postmenopausal bleeding, endometrium ≥4–5 mm→hysteroscopy + biopsy
4Ovarian masses, ectopic signs, and consent

TVUS characterises ovarian masses and feeds the IOTA rules (simple benign vs malignant features). In suspected ectopic, look for an adnexal mass, the tubal 'ring', and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. TVUS is intimate: it needs informed consent and a chaperone every time.

🔎IOTA rules
Simple/benign vs malignant ultrasound features to triage ovarian masses.
💍Tubal ring
Echogenic adnexal ring separate from the ovary suggests tubal ectopic.
🚫When not to use
Not sexually active, speculum not tolerated, or declined — use transabdominal instead.
🚩 An empty uterus on TVUS with a positive pregnancy test is a pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) — treat as ectopic until proven otherwise. Arrange gynaecology review and serial serum hCG; never reassure the patient home without a plan.
🎓 TVUS is the detail scan with an empty bladder; transabdominal is the overview scan with a full bladder. Confirm an intrauterine pregnancy and you have all but excluded ectopic — but an empty uterus with positive hCG is ectopic/PUL until proven otherwise.

Pelvic ultrasound is the first-line imaging test for the uterus and endometrium. Transabdominal scanning surveys size, position and gross pathology, but the endometrial stripe and myometrial detail are best resolved on the transvaginal (TV) approach, which sits the probe close to the uterus. The single most important measurement you will report is the endometrial thickness — and in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding, it is the number that either reassures or triggers an urgent cancer pathway.

1Systematic uterine assessment

Describe the uterus in a fixed order so nothing is missed: size (longitudinal x AP x transverse), position — anteverted (fundus tips forward, the common position) or retroverted (fundus tips back toward the sacrum) — the myometrium (normally homogeneous, mid-grey), and the endometrial stripe. On TV sagittal the endometrium is the bright central line; the surrounding hypoechoic halo is the inner myometrium (junctional zone).

Endometrial stripe poorly seen transabdominally→proceed to transvaginal scan for accurate stripe measurement
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
2Myometrial pathology: fibroids vs adenomyosis

Two everyday causes of a bulky uterus and heavy bleeding look quite different on ultrasound.

🧬Fibroid (leiomyoma)
Well-defined, rounded hypoechoic myometrial mass with a whorled texture; may cast acoustic shadowing. Classified by site — subserosal, intramural, or submucosal (the last distorts the cavity and causes menorrhagia). May calcify (bright with shadow) or degenerate (cystic/heterogeneous).
🌀Adenomyosis
Diffusely enlarged, "globular" uterus with heterogeneous myometrium, myometrial cysts, and a poorly defined / thickened junctional zone. No discrete mass. Asymmetric myometrial wall thickening with radiating shadows.
Fibroids are focal and well-defined; adenomyosis is diffuse and ill-defined.
Submucosal fibroids matter most for bleeding and fertility because they intrude on the cavity.
3Endometrial thickness — the key measurement

Endometrial thickness is measured as the double-layer (both endometrial surfaces) at its widest point on the TV sagittal/midline image, excluding any hypoechoic halo and excluding intracavity fluid. In premenopausal women the endometrium changes across the cycle — thin and bright just after menses (proliferative), thicker and more echogenic in the secretory phase — so there is no single "normal" number; interpret against cycle day.

Postmenopausal bleeding, endometrium ≤4 mm→reassuring — endometrial cancer very unlikely
Postmenopausal bleeding, endometrium >4 mm→hysteroscopy + endometrial biopsy (pipelle) to exclude carcinoma
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image.
4Focal lesions, anomalies and devices

An endometrial polyp shows as focal echogenic thickening within the cavity, often with a single feeding vessel on Doppler. When the stripe is equivocal, saline infusion sonography (sonohysterography) distends the cavity with sterile saline to outline polyps, submucosal fibroids and adhesions. Congenital anomalies — bicornuate (two divergent horns, external fundal cleft) or septate (single external contour, internal septum) — are best characterised on a 3D coronal view. An IUCD is a bright, shadowing linear echo that should sit centrally within the endometrial cavity; report malposition (low-lying, embedded in myometrium, or perforating).

A Doppler feeding vessel favours a polyp over a blood clot (clot has no flow).
Bicornuate = external contour splits; septate = external contour intact — the distinction drives management.
🚩 Postmenopausal bleeding with a thickened endometrium (>4 mm) is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Refer on a 2-week-wait suspected-cancer gynaecology pathway for hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy — do not attribute the bleeding to atrophy on ultrasound alone.
🎓 The 4 mm cut-off applies specifically to the postmenopausal woman with bleeding: below it, cancer is very unlikely and you can reassure; above it, tissue is mandatory. It is not a screening threshold for the asymptomatic postmenopausal endometrium, where an incidentally thickened stripe is interpreted more conservatively.

The ovary is the most versatile organ on a pelvic ultrasound — home to physiological follicles, benign cysts, sinister masses, and one true surgical emergency. Learn to read the adnexa systematically: characterise the cyst, apply the IOTA/RMI rules to solid masses, and never miss a torsion.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: normal transvaginal ovary, oval and slightly hypoechoic, studded with several small anechoic antral follicles giving the classic "chocolate-chip cookie" appearance.
1The normal ovary

Almond-shaped, ~3 × 2 × 2 cm in a woman of reproductive age, with a normal volume <10 mL. It contains multiple small anechoic follicles arranged peripherally. A dominant follicle may reach ~2–2.5 cm before ovulation. After the menopause the ovary shrinks and becomes follicle-free and hard to visualise — any prominent post-menopausal ovarian mass deserves extra suspicion.

Anechoic, thin-walled, round structure with posterior acoustic enhancement→simple cyst — almost always benign/functional
2Characterising ovarian cysts

Cyst characterisation is pattern recognition. Four appearances cover the vast majority of what you will be shown:

💧Simple cyst
Anechoic, thin smooth wall, no septa, posterior enhancement. Functional (follicular or corpus luteal). Benign; resolves — repeat scan in 6–12 weeks.
🩸Haemorrhagic cyst
Lace-like / reticular ("fishnet" or "cobweb") internal echoes from fibrin strands, sometimes a retracting clot. No internal Doppler flow. Resolves.
🧬Dermoid / mature teratoma
Echogenic focus with fat, calcification and hair; "tip of the iceberg" shadowing obscures the deep border. Benign but often removed.
🍫Endometrioma
"Chocolate cyst" — homogeneous low-level "ground-glass" echoes, no solid vascular nodule. Marker of endometriosis.
A cyst that is not simple is not automatically sinister — the reticular echoes of a haemorrhagic cyst and the ground-glass of an endometrioma are both reassuringly benign patterns. Malignancy is suggested by solid vascular tissue, not just internal echoes.
3Polycystic ovaries

The updated Rotterdam threshold is ≥20 follicles per ovary (2–9 mm) and/or an increased ovarian volume (>10 mL), often with a peripheral "string of pearls" arrangement and dense central stroma.

Polycystic morphology on ultrasound alone→does NOT diagnose PCOS
PCOS is a clinical–biochemical diagnosis (Rotterdam: two of three — oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic morphology). Many normal young women have polycystic-appearing ovaries with no syndrome, so never report "PCOS" from the scan alone.
4Features of malignancy — IOTA & RMI

The worrying features of an adnexal mass are: solid components, thick (>3 mm) septations, papillary projections (≥4), bilaterality, ascites, and high internal Doppler flow. These feed two commonly used tools:

IOTA simple rules apply five benign (B) and five malignant (M) features; the mass is classified benign, malignant, or inconclusive.
RMI = U × M × CA-125. U = ultrasound score (0/1/3 from multilocularity, solid areas, bilaterality, ascites, metastases); M = menopausal status (1 pre, 3 post); CA-125 in U/mL. RMI >200 → gynae-oncology referral.
Complex solid mass + ascites + raised CA-125→high RMI → 2-week-wait gynae-oncology MDT
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: enlarged oedematous ovary displaced medially with peripheralised follicles, and a colour-Doppler box showing a twisted "whirlpool sign" pedicle with absent central arterial flow — ovarian torsion.
5Torsion & tubo-ovarian abscess

Ovarian torsion: an enlarged, oedematous ovary (often on a lead-point cyst/dermoid), peripherally displaced follicles, a "whirlpool sign" of the twisted vascular pedicle, and absent or reduced Doppler flow. Crucially, flow may still be present because the ovary has dual blood supply — a normal Doppler does not exclude torsion, so clinical suspicion overrides the scan.

Fever, PID, tender complex adnexal mass with thick walls and debris→tubo-ovarian abscess — IV antibiotics ± drainage
🚩 Ovarian torsion is a gynaecological emergency. Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea/vomiting and an adnexal mass — even if Doppler flow is preserved — needs urgent gynae review and diagnostic laparoscopy to detorse and save the ovary. Do not wait for imaging to "confirm" absent flow. Separately, any suspicious complex mass with ascites should trigger CA-125, RMI calculation, and referral to the gynae-oncology MDT — never simply reassure and discharge.
🎓 Anechoic + thin-walled + posterior enhancement = simple functional cyst (leave it alone). Ground-glass = endometrioma; tip-of-the-iceberg shadow = dermoid; lace-like echoes = haemorrhagic cyst. Solid vascular tissue, thick septa, papillae and ascites are the malignant company you keep. And the one you must never miss is torsion — where the patient's pain, not the Doppler, makes the call.

A woman presents with pain and/or bleeding in the first trimester. The single question that drives everything is: where is the pregnancy, and is it viable? Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) in the Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit (EPAU) is first-line, read alongside serum hCG.

1Confirm the location — is there an intrauterine pregnancy?

TVUS is preferred over transabdominal scanning: the probe sits closer to the pelvic organs, giving far better resolution of early landmarks. The first job is simply to find a pregnancy inside the uterine cavity. A positive urine/serum hCG with an empty uterus is not reassuring — it is a pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) until proven otherwise.

Empty uterus + positive pregnancy test→pregnancy of unknown location — actively exclude ectopic
2Know the normal landmarks by gestation

Early structures appear in a predictable order. Memorising the sequence lets you say whether a scan is normal-for-dates or worrying.

Intrauterine gestational sac — visible from ~4.5–5 weeks. Should sit eccentrically within the decidua.
Yolk sac — from ~5.5 weeks. The first structure confirming a true intrauterine pregnancy.
Fetal pole with heartbeat — from ~6 weeks. Cardiac activity confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: transvaginal view of an intrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac (thin echogenic ring) and an early fetal pole, sac sitting eccentrically within the decidua.
3Use the discriminatory zone to interpret an empty uterus

The discriminatory zone is the serum hCG level above which an intrauterine sac should be seen transvaginally — roughly >1500 IU/L. If hCG is above this threshold and the uterus is empty, an ectopic becomes far more likely.

Serum hCG >~1500 IU/L, no intrauterine sac on TVUS→raises suspicion of ectopic pregnancy

Below the threshold or when the picture is uncertain, use serial hCG: a normal intrauterine pregnancy roughly doubles over 48 hours, whereas a suboptimal (slow) rise supports an ectopic. A fall suggests a failing PUL/miscarriage.

4Apply the miscarriage criteria (NICE/RCOG)

When an intrauterine pregnancy is present but may be failing, strict thresholds prevent misdiagnosing a viable pregnancy as lost. A pregnancy is non-viable if:

Fetal pole crown-rump length ≥7 mm with no heartbeat.
Mean gestational sac diameter ≥25 mm with no fetal pole (empty sac).
If measurements are below these thresholds, or there is any uncertainty: rescan in 7–14 days before diagnosing miscarriage.

Types of miscarriage: threatened (bleeding, closed os, viable pregnancy); missed (early fetal demise — non-viable pregnancy retained, often no symptoms); incomplete (some products retained); complete (uterus emptied).

5Recognise ectopic and molar sonographic signs

For an ectopic, the uterus is typically empty; look actively at the adnexa and the pouch of Douglas.

◎Tubal ring / bagel sign
Adnexal mass with an echogenic ring, seen separate from the ovary — moves independently on probe pressure.
≈Free fluid in pouch of Douglas
Anechoic or echogenic fluid suggests haemoperitoneum — worrying for rupture.
○Pseudogestational sac
Central fluid collection within the cavity that mimics a sac — no yolk sac, no eccentric position. Do not be reassured.
❄Molar — snowstorm
"Snowstorm" / cluster-of-grapes appearance with markedly raised hCG — hydatidiform mole.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: adnexal "bagel"/tubal ring sign lying separate from the ipsilateral ovary, with free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.
🚩 Ruptured ectopic is a life-threatening surgical emergency. A haemodynamically unstable woman (tachycardia, hypotension, collapse) with a positive pregnancy test, free fluid/haemoperitoneum, or shoulder-tip pain must be resuscitated and taken to theatre — never delay for imaging in the unstable patient. Call senior gynae help immediately, secure large-bore IV access, cross-match, and prepare for laparoscopy/laparotomy.
🎓 An empty uterus with a positive pregnancy test is a pregnancy of unknown location, not a reassuring scan — pair TVUS with serum hCG and the discriminatory zone, and remember that a stable patient gets imaged and monitored while an unstable one goes straight to resuscitation and theatre.

The bladder is the easiest organ to scan and one of the highest-yield: a bedside probe or automated bladder scanner answers a single decisive question — how full is it? Volume and post-void residual (PVR) tell you whether a deteriorating, anuric or catheter-dependent patient is obstructed, retaining, or simply dry.

1Estimating bladder volume — the ellipsoid formula
The bladder is modelled as an ellipsoid. Measure three orthogonal diameters — height (craniocaudal, sagittal view), width (transverse) and depth (anteroposterior) — and multiply:
Volume (mL) ≈ height × width × depth × 0.52 (all in cm).
Automated bladder scanners perform this internally across several planes and display a number directly. Full bladder = anechoic (black) fluid with posterior acoustic enhancement, thin smooth wall.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: transverse suprapubic view of a full bladder as an anechoic square-ish structure with calipers marking width and depth, thin regular wall, bright posterior acoustic enhancement behind it.
2Post-void residual (PVR)
Ask the patient to void, then scan immediately (delay lets urine re-accumulate and falsely raises the number). PVR quantifies emptying:
PVR <50 mL→normal emptying
PVR up to ~100 mL→acceptable, esp. in the elderly
PVR persistently raised→incomplete emptying — outlet obstruction (BPH), neurogenic bladder, detrusor underactivity or anticholinergic/opioid medication
A single mildly raised PVR can be artefactual — repeat before acting.
Bladder scanners over-read when a large ovarian cyst, ascites or gravid uterus sits in the field; confirm with real-time imaging if the number is implausible.
3Acute vs chronic retention
Acute urinary retention: sudden, painful inability to void; palpable/percussable distended bladder; scan typically >600 mL. Confirm and quantify by bladder scan, then catheterise and record the drained residual volume.
Chronic retention: large-volume, often painless retention that develops insidiously. Can generate high intravesical pressure → bilateral hydronephrosis and post-obstructive AKI. After catheterisation watch for post-obstructive diuresis and electrolyte shifts.
💧Raised PVR
Incomplete emptying — obstruction, neurogenic, detrusor underactivity, drugs.
🧱Wall thickening / trabeculation
Chronic outflow obstruction; may see diverticula.
⚪Bladder stone
Echogenic, mobile, casts acoustic shadow — moves with position.
🔴Bladder tumour
Non-mobile wall-based soft-tissue mass; does not shift with position.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: grossly distended thick-walled trabeculated bladder in chronic retention, with a mobile echogenic stone casting a posterior shadow and paired split-screen kidney showing dilated calyces (hydronephrosis).
4Clinical uses at the bedside
Avoid unnecessary catheterisation (and its infection risk); distinguish anuria from retention in the deteriorating or oliguric patient; monitor emptying after catheter removal; and guide the timing of intermittent self-catheterisation in neurogenic bladder.
🚩 A distended bladder with bilateral hydronephrosis and a rising creatinine = high-pressure chronic retention with obstructive AKI. Catheterise urgently, then monitor closely for post-obstructive diuresis and electrolyte disturbance.
🎓 The number on the scanner only means something if the timing is right: a "high residual" measured 20 minutes after voiding is often just a re-filling bladder. Scan immediately post-void, repeat a borderline value, and always interpret volume alongside the wall, the kidneys and the creatinine — not in isolation.
ULTRASOUND__Obstetric:
The dating scan is the first routine antenatal ultrasound, offered to every woman in the UK between 11+2 and 14+1 weeks. It has four jobs: confirm a viable intrauterine pregnancy, accurately date the pregnancy and set the estimated due date (EDD), establish chorionicity in multiple pregnancy, and screen for gross early anomalies. Scan-based dating supersedes LMP-based dates and standardises the timing of all later screening.

1Confirm viability and intrauterine location

The first questions are the most fundamental: is there a pregnancy, is it inside the uterine cavity, and is it alive? A fetal heartbeat should be visible from around 6 weeks, so by the dating window a heartbeat is expected. Absence of cardiac activity with a fetal pole of appropriate size raises the possibility of a missed (silent) miscarriage. An empty uterus with a positive pregnancy test should prompt urgent thought about ectopic pregnancy.

No fetal heartbeat with a fetal pole present→suspect missed miscarriage; arrange rescan / specialist review
2Date the pregnancy with crown-rump length (CRL)

Dating is the defining purpose of this scan. In the first trimester the crown-rump length (CRL) — the straight-line measurement from the top of the head to the bottom of the rump — is the single most accurate way to date a pregnancy, reliable from roughly 8.5 to 14 weeks. Before ~8.5 weeks the gestational sac / early CRL is used; once CRL exceeds ~84 mm (beyond ~14 weeks) it becomes unreliable and head circumference (HC) takes over. Whatever the LMP said, the scan date wins and resets the EDD.

CRL is measured in a true mid-sagittal plane with the fetus in a neutral (non-flexed, non-extended) position.
A significant mismatch between scan dates and LMP dates is expected and the scan takes precedence — but a very large discrepancy should be flagged.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: a mid-sagittal view of the fetus with electronic calipers positioned at the crown and the rump measuring the crown-rump length.
3Determine chorionicity and amnionicity in twins

If more than one fetus is present, the most important task is to establish chorionicity (number of placentas) and amnionicity (number of amniotic sacs). This is done most accurately in the first trimester, which is one reason the dating scan matters so much for twins. The membrane insertion at the placenta gives the answer: a thick, triangular wedge of placental tissue between the membranes — the lambda / twin-peak sign — indicates a dichorionic pregnancy, whereas a thin membrane meeting the placenta at a right angle with no wedge — the T-sign — indicates a monochorionic pregnancy.

λLambda / twin-peak sign
Triangular placental wedge between membranes = dichorionic (two placentas). Lower-risk twin type.
TT-sign
Membrane meets placenta at 90° with no wedge = monochorionic (shared placenta). Risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: a twin pregnancy showing the intertwin membrane meeting the placenta, contrasting the triangular lambda/twin-peak sign of a dichorionic pair with the flat T-sign of a monochorionic pair.
4Screen for early anomalies and offer combined screening

The dating scan also allows detection of some gross structural anomalies (for example anencephaly or major body-wall defects) and is the natural point at which to offer first-trimester combined screening, which includes measurement of the nuchal translucency together with maternal serum markers to estimate the chance of trisomy 21, 18 and 13. Accurate CRL dating is what makes this screening valid, because the risk calculation is gestation-dependent.

🚩 A large discrepancy between scan dates and LMP, absence of a fetal heartbeat (possible missed miscarriage), or a multiple pregnancy found to be monochorionic all warrant escalation. Monochorionic twins carry the risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and require increased surveillance under a specialist fetal medicine team.
🎓 Remember the four C's of the dating scan: Cardiac activity (viability), Cavity (intrauterine location), CRL (accurate dating, best 8.5–14 weeks), and Chorionicity (lambda = dichorionic, T = monochorionic). CRL is the most accurate dating tool of the whole pregnancy — after 14 weeks its throne passes to head circumference.

Nuchal translucency (NT) is the ultrasound-measured anechoic fluid space at the back of the fetal neck. It is one component of the UK first-trimester combined screening test for chromosomal abnormality, offered to all pregnant women between 11+2 and 14+1 weeks. Screening estimates a chance of a condition; it does not diagnose it.

1What NT measures and why it matters

NT is the maximal thickness of the subcutaneous translucent fluid layer between the skin and soft tissue overlying the cervical spine. It is measured on a mid-sagittal fetal image with the neck neutral. NT normally increases with crown-rump length (CRL), so results are interpreted for gestation, not against a single fixed number.

An increased NT (typically >3.5 mm, or raised for CRL) is associated with:

  • Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
  • Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) and Patau syndrome (trisomy 13)
  • Congenital cardiac defects and other structural anomalies
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: mid-sagittal fetal profile at ~12 weeks with calipers placed on the anechoic nuchal fluid space, showing NT measurement.
2The combined test

The combined test integrates three inputs into a single risk figure:

Maternal age + NT + serum biochemistry (β-hCG, PAPP-A)→a numerical chance (e.g. 1 in 300) of trisomy 21/18/13

The characteristic first-trimester biochemistry in trisomy 21 is raised β-hCG and low PAPP-A (pregnancy-associated plasma protein A).

A "higher-chance" result is commonly defined as a risk ≥1 in 150. This prompts the offer of further testing.
A "lower-chance" result does not exclude a condition — it means the estimated chance falls below the cut-off.
3After a higher-chance result

A higher-chance result leads to the offer of definitive diagnostic testing, or non-invasive testing as an intermediate step. Screening itself carries no procedure risk; the invasive diagnostic tests carry a small miscarriage risk of roughly 0.5–1%.

🧬NIPT (cfDNA)
Non-invasive prenatal test on cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood. Highly sensitive screen, no procedure risk — an intermediate option before invasive testing.
🔬CVS
Chorionic villus sampling, from ~11–14 weeks. Diagnostic karyotype from placental tissue; small miscarriage risk.
💧Amniocentesis
From ~15 weeks onward. Diagnostic karyotype from amniotic fluid; small miscarriage risk.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: markedly increased nuchal translucency (>3.5 mm) with a large anechoic space, contrasted alongside a normal NT for reference.
4If screening is missed or booked late

NT can only be measured within the 11+2 to 14+1 window. If a woman books late or the window is missed, the alternative is the second-trimester quadruple test (14–20 weeks), which screens for trisomy 21 only using maternal serum (AFP, hCG, uE3, inhibin A).

Where NT is increased but the karyotype is normal, the fetus remains at higher risk of cardiac and structural anomalies — detailed fetal cardiac scanning is still warranted.

🚩 A markedly increased NT or a higher-chance combined-test result requires sensitive, non-directive counselling and referral to fetal medicine for diagnostic testing and specialist follow-up. Never present a screening result as a diagnosis.
🎓 Remember the logic chain: NT is one input, not an answer. Combined test (age + NT + β-hCG↑ + PAPP-A↓) gives a chance; a result ≥1 in 150 offers NIPT or diagnostic CVS/amniocentesis. Screening carries no risk; diagnosis carries a ~0.5–1% miscarriage risk. Miss the window → quadruple test for T21 only.

The 20-week anomaly scan (fetal anomaly scan / mid-trimester scan) is offered to every pregnant woman in the UK between 18+0 and 20+6 weeks under the NHS Fetal Anomaly Screening Programme (FASP). It is a systematic head-to-toe structural survey of fetal anatomy, plus assessment of placental location and liquor volume. Crucially it is a screening test — a normal scan reduces but never abolishes the chance of an anomaly, and detection depends on the condition, maternal habitus and fetal position.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: standard transventricular axial view of the fetal head showing the cavum septum pellucidum, thalami and posterior horns of the lateral ventricles for atrial measurement.
1Head & brain
Assess skull shape and ossification, the cavum septum pellucidum, lateral ventricles (atrial width, normally <10 mm), midline falx, and the cerebellum with cisterna magna. Look for anencephaly/acrania, ventriculomegaly and posterior fossa abnormalities.
2Face & spine
Inspect the upper lip and profile for cleft lip. Sweep the spine in sagittal, coronal and transverse planes for neural tube defects (spina bifida) and skin integrity over the vertebrae.
Scalloped frontal bones + obliterated cisterna magna with cerebellum wrapped back→the "lemon" (skull) and "banana" (cerebellum) signs of open spina bifida
3Heart
Confirm situs and a symmetrical four-chamber view, then the left and right ventricular outflow tracts. Serious cardiac anomalies are among the hardest conditions to detect and depend heavily on fetal position and operator skill.
4Abdomen, kidneys & wall
Check a fluid-filled stomach in the left upper quadrant, both kidneys and the bladder, and cord insertion into an intact abdominal wall.
Herniated bowel/liver covered by a membranous sac at the cord insertion = exomphalos (associated with aneuploidy).
Free-floating loops of uncovered bowel to the right of the cord = gastroschisis (usually isolated).
5Limbs, placenta & liquor
Confirm three long bones in each limb and the presence of hands and feet. Document placental location and amniotic fluid volume.
Low-lying placenta reaching or covering the internal os at 20 weeks→flag for a repeat transvaginal scan at ~32–36 weeks to assess for placenta praevia

FASP specifically audits detection of 11 conditions: anencephaly, open spina bifida, cleft lip, diaphragmatic hernia, exomphalos, gastroschisis, serious cardiac anomalies, bilateral renal agenesis, lethal skeletal dysplasia, Edwards' syndrome (trisomy 18) and Patau's syndrome (trisomy 13).

🧠Echogenic bowel
Bowel as bright as bone; consider CF, congenital infection, swallowed blood or aneuploidy.
❤️Echogenic intracardiac focus
Bright spot in a ventricle (usually left); weak isolated marker for trisomy 21.
💧Mild pyelectasis
Renal pelvis dilatation ≥4 mm; prompts third-trimester follow-up ± aneuploidy context.
🔵Choroid plexus cyst
Cyst within choroid plexus; in isolation benign, but a soft marker for trisomy 18.

Soft markers are minor, often transient findings that are not anomalies in themselves but may prompt reassessment of aneuploidy risk in the context of the woman's earlier combined-test result. In isolation most require no action beyond documentation.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: transverse abdominal wall view showing free-floating loops of uncovered bowel in the amniotic fluid to the right of a normal cord insertion, consistent with gastroschisis.
🚩 Detection of a major structural anomaly mandates prompt referral to a fetal medicine unit for detailed assessment, counselling and multidisciplinary planning. Anhydramnios with an absent bladder and non-visualised or absent kidneys suggests bilateral renal agenesis — a lethal anomaly (Potter sequence) — and needs urgent specialist review.
🎓 A normal 20-week scan is reassuring but never a guarantee: it is screening, not diagnosis. Detection rates vary by condition and are limited by fetal lie and maternal body habitus, so always frame the result to the woman as reducing — not eliminating — the chance of an abnormality.

A growth scan is a third-trimester ultrasound performed for a clinical indication — not a routine offer to every pregnancy — to answer two linked questions: is the fetus the right size, and is it well? It pairs fetal biometry (to estimate weight and plot a centile) with markers of placental function (liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler). Its main job is to catch the small, compromised fetus at risk of stillbirth in time to intervene.

1Who gets a growth scan — the indications
Growth scans are triggered by concern, not by protocol for all. Common reasons: a symphysis-fundal height (SFH) measuring small or large for dates or crossing centiles on the customised chart; reduced fetal movements; and maternal risk factors that threaten placental function — chronic hypertension or pre-eclampsia, diabetes (pre-existing or gestational), a previous SGA baby or stillbirth, and multiple pregnancy. These pregnancies are placed on a schedule of serial scans so that trajectory, not just a single snapshot, can be judged.
2Biometry and estimated fetal weight (EFW)
Four standard measurements are taken and combined into an estimated fetal weight, then plotted as a centile on a customised or population growth chart:
Biparietal diameter (BPD) — outer-to-inner across the fetal skull at the level of the thalami.
Head circumference (HC) — around the same axial plane; relatively spared in placental insufficiency.
Abdominal circumference (AC) — at the level of the stomach and umbilical vein; the single most sensitive measure for growth restriction, as it reflects liver glycogen and fat stores.
Femur length (FL) — the ossified diaphysis of the femur.

3Fetal growth restriction (FGR / IUGR)
FGR is defined as an EFW or AC below the 10th centile, and is more concerning when the trajectory is falling or static across serial scans. In placental insufficiency the pattern is often asymmetric — the brain is preferentially perfused, so HC is preserved while AC drops ("head-sparing"). A key distinction is between the constitutionally small-but-healthy fetus and the truly compromised one, which is why biometry alone is never enough.
AC low + HC preserved + abnormal Doppler→asymmetric FGR from placental insufficiency
4Wellbeing: liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler
Size is coupled with function. Liquor volume is quantified as the amniotic fluid index (AFI) or single deepest vertical pool; oligohydramnios reflects reduced fetal renal perfusion and points to placental insufficiency. Umbilical artery Doppler assesses placental resistance: normally there is forward flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Rising resistance, then absent, then reversed end-diastolic flow (AREDF) marks progressive placental compromise and correlates with deteriorating fetal status.

5The other extreme: macrosomia / LGA
Large-for-gestational-age is an EFW above the 90th centile, classically associated with maternal diabetes (fetal hyperinsulinaemia drives excess growth, often with a disproportionately large AC). The main intrapartum concern is shoulder dystocia. As with FGR, serial scans usually spaced ≥2 weeks apart track the trajectory and inform delivery planning.
📏AC
Most sensitive single measure for growth restriction; falls first in asymmetric FGR.
💧Oligohydramnios
Reduced liquor signals placental insufficiency and reduced fetal renal perfusion.
🌊AREDF
Absent/reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler = severe placental compromise.
🚩 A growth-restricted fetus with absent or reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler and/or oligohydramnios indicates placental insufficiency and a real risk of stillbirth. This needs urgent fetal medicine input, antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity, and consideration of timed delivery — do not simply rebook a routine interval scan.
🎓 A single low centile can be a healthy small baby; it is the trajectory plus Dopplers and liquor that separate constitutional smallness from a failing placenta. When AC lags but HC holds, think head-sparing asymmetric FGR and look hard at the umbilical artery.

Fetal Doppler ultrasound interrogates the fetoplacental circulation to monitor a fetus that is growth-restricted or otherwise at risk. By sampling flow in the umbilical artery, middle cerebral artery, ductus venosus and uterine arteries you build a picture of placental function, fetal adaptation to hypoxia, and the timing of safe delivery.

1Umbilical artery (UA) — the frontline surveillance tool in FGR

The UA reflects downstream placental resistance. A healthy placenta is a low-resistance bed, so there is continuous forward flow throughout diastole. As villous vasculature is progressively obliterated, diastolic flow falls and the pulsatility index (PI) rises. Deterioration follows an ominous, ordered sequence:

Rising placental resistance→Raised PI → Absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) → Reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF)

AEDF and REDF signal severe placental insufficiency with a high risk of fetal hypoxia, acidaemia and stillbirth. REDF is the most advanced arterial sign and mandates urgent fetal medicine input.

Normal UA: sawtooth waveform with generous forward flow filling diastole; low PI.
AEDF: the trace touches the baseline in diastole — no forward flow at end-diastole.
REDF: the diastolic component dips below the baseline — flow reverses back towards the fetus.

2Middle cerebral artery (MCA) — brain-sparing and fetal anaemia

The hypoxic fetus preferentially redistributes cardiac output to the brain, myocardium and adrenals — the brain-sparing effect. Cerebral vasodilation drops the MCA PI, so a falling MCA PI is an early marker of centralisation.

The cerebroplacental ratio (CPR = MCA PI ÷ UA PI) combines both territories: a low CPR flags redistribution and predicts adverse perinatal outcome, sometimes before individual vessels become abnormal.

Separately, MCA peak systolic velocity (PSV) rises in fetal anaemia (low blood viscosity and high-output state). A PSV >1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) is the trigger to arrange intrauterine transfusion.

Rhesus/red-cell alloimmunisation or parvovirus B19→Fetal anaemia → raised MCA PSV → time intrauterine transfusion
3Ductus venosus & uterine artery — late signs and prediction

The ductus venosus (DV) shunts oxygenated blood to the heart; its waveform reflects right atrial pressure and cardiac function. An absent or reversed a-wave is a late, pre-terminal sign of myocardial decompensation and is used to time delivery in very preterm FGR.

The uterine artery reflects maternal-side trophoblast invasion of the spiral arteries. Persistently high resistance with early diastolic "notching" (typically assessed in the second trimester) predicts pre-eclampsia and FGR.

🩸Umbilical artery
Placental resistance. Raised PI → AEDF → REDF marks worsening insufficiency.
🧠MCA PI / CPR
Low PI = brain-sparing; low CPR = redistribution and adverse outcome.
💉MCA PSV
Raised in fetal anaemia; >1.5 MoM times intrauterine transfusion.
❤️Ductus venosus
Absent/reversed a-wave = late, pre-terminal sign; times preterm delivery.
🩺Uterine artery
High resistance with diastolic notching predicts pre-eclampsia and FGR.

🚩 Absent or reversed umbilical artery end-diastolic flow indicates critical placental compromise — arrange urgent fetal medicine review, give antenatal corticosteroids, and consider delivery. A reversed ductus venosus a-wave signals imminent fetal decompensation.
🎓 Think of it as a staged story: the umbilical artery tells you how sick the placenta is (PI → AEDF → REDF), the MCA tells you how the fetus is coping (brain-sparing, low CPR), and the ductus venosus tells you the fetus is running out of time (reversed a-wave). MCA PSV is the odd one out — it is about anaemia, not hypoxia.

The biophysical profile (BPP) is an ultrasound-based composite test of fetal wellbeing used in high-risk pregnancies and suspected fetal compromise. It combines acute markers of fetal oxygenation (activities controlled by the fetal CNS) with a marker of chronic placental function (amniotic fluid). Five components, each scored 2 (normal) or 0 (abnormal), give a maximum of 10.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: transabdominal sagittal view of the fetal trunk showing the diaphragm, used to observe rhythmic fetal breathing movements over the observation window.
1The five components (each scored 2 or 0)

Each parameter is observed over up to 30 minutes. Score 2 if the defined criterion is met, 0 if not.

🫁Fetal breathing
≥1 episode of rhythmic breathing lasting ≥30 seconds.
🤸Gross body movements
≥3 discrete body or limb movements.
💪Fetal tone
≥1 episode of active extension then return to flexion (e.g. hand opening/closing).
💧Amniotic fluid volume
Single deepest vertical pool ≥2 cm.
📈Reactive CTG (NST)
Reactive non-stress test with accelerations.

Modified BPP uses just two components — amniotic fluid volume + CTG (NST) — as a quicker screening test.

2Interpreting the score
Score 8–10→Reassuring / normal — low risk of fetal hypoxia; routine surveillance.
Score 6→Equivocal — repeat within 24h or deliver depending on gestation and clinical context.
Score ≤4→Abnormal — strong evidence of fetal hypoxia; usually prompts delivery.
Oligohydramnios (deepest pool <2 cm) is significant even with an otherwise normal score, as it reflects chronic placental insufficiency and warrants closer surveillance or delivery.
3Physiological basis — gradual hypoxia

The biophysical activities are driven by fetal CNS centres with differing sensitivity to hypoxia. Centres that develop earliest are most resistant, so they fail last:

Lost first→CTG reactivity and fetal breathing movements (most hypoxia-sensitive).
Lost later→Gross body movements, then finally fetal tone (most resistant).

Amniotic fluid is different — it reflects chronic placental function: sustained hypoxia redistributes fetal blood flow away from the kidneys, reducing urine output and causing oligohydramnios. The BPP is therefore used alongside umbilical artery Dopplers and growth assessment in the surveillance of fetal growth restriction (FGR).

📷 Image placeholder — describe the ultrasound image: measurement of the single deepest vertical pool of amniotic fluid, callipers spanning a fluid pocket free of cord and fetal parts, to assess amniotic fluid volume.
🚩 A low BPP score (≤4), especially with oligohydramnios or absent fetal breathing/movements, indicates significant fetal hypoxia and usually mandates urgent delivery after fetal medicine review. Do not delay escalation.
🎓 Remember the order fetal activities are lost in hypoxia with the idea that the last skill acquired is the first lost: breathing and CTG reactivity fail early, while tone — present from earliest development — is preserved until severe compromise. A normal BPP is strongly reassuring, but oligohydramnios always deserves attention as a marker of chronic placental failure.
